newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: FEATURE - Slovenia, with eye on EU, set for turn to right.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Slovenia, with eye on EU, set for turn to right.

text.p: Slovenia, its past as an integral part of former Yugoslavia almost a distant memory, faces its second general election on Sunday with its heart set on membership of NATO and the European Union.

Politically stable with an impressive set of democratic credentials, the mountainous state has gone a long way in its five years of independence to transform its communist command economy into a free market, while maintaining a healthy standard of living for its two million inhabitants.

Politicians of all colours, and many ordinary Slovenians, refer to Mitteleuropa (Central Europe) as their natural home after being forced for decades to pay homage to the Yugoslav federation at the heart of the Balkans.

There is irony in the fact that much of Slovenia's success has been attributed to Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, who once wielded power as president of Yugoslavia in the city of Belgrade regarded by many Slovenians with barely-concealed disdain.

With a firm hand on the government tiller, Drnovsek and his centre-left Liberal Democrats have juggled since the last election in 1992 with an array of coalition partners without the need to resort to early elections.
Drnovsek crowned his premiership in June by finalising associate membership with the European Union, the first step towards entry into the Brussels club. Ljubljana wants to join by 2001.
Slovenia has also recently emerged as a strong contender to be among the first ex-communist states to join the NATO military alliance with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Political analysts believe the Liberal Democrats (LDS) will clinch the highest number of votes in Sunday's election and that Drnovsek will remain prime minister.

Drnovsek was most likely to form a coalition with rightist parties more willing to take some of the tough economic decisions to prepare Slovenia for EU membership and the Maastricht treaty on European economic and monetary union.

"The Liberal Democrats are most likely to stay in coalition with the Christian Democrats (SKD), but a partnership with the People's Party (SLS) is also possible," Igor Luksic, professor of politics at Ljubljana's Faculty of Social Sciences, told Reuters.

Drnovsek had included the former communists, now known as the United List of Social Democrats, in his government after the 1992 general election, but the leftists quit in January in a row over economic and social policies.
"The United List seems to be the last option for the Liberal Democrats because it puts too much emphasis on social issues," Luksic said.
Slovenia's 1.5 million voters will have some 28 parties to choose from in the November 10 election, but only up to 10 are likely to make it into the 90-seat lower house of parliament.
Latest opinion polls show the Liberal Democrats with around 15 to 22 percent support, followed by the rightist People's Party, the farmers' champion, with between nine and 10 percent.
The Social Democratic Party, also on the right, is steady with around eight percent.
The party is led by fiery former defence minister Janez Jansa, who earned hero status by orchestrating the 10-day independence war against Yugoslav federal troops in June 1991.

The United List of Social Democrats have between five and seven percent backing, while some six percent of voters say they will support the Christian Democrats. Around a third of the electorate was still undecided.
Experts agree that Slovenia's next government will gradually have to cut welfare benefits, trim pensions and reduce spending on education and health.
"The new government will have to implement some changes (regarding social benefits), no matter who will be in it," said Drago Zajc, a researcher at Ljubljana's Faculty of Social Sciences.

Drnovsek's government has also pledged to speed up the pace of privatisation but many foreign investors have been irked by Slovenia's reticence to cut bureaucracy and introduce more investor-friendly legislation.
Such measures, including the disposal of loss-making state concerns, spell a period of pain for Slovenians.
Despite income per capita of around $9,500, already higher than Greece and Portugal, Slovenian workers have held a series of strikes this year over higher pay.

Labour unrest is likely to remain a thorn in the side of the Ljubljana government should the unemployment rate increase above its current rate of around 13.5 percent without the cushioning of a social safety net.
While surveys show most Slovenians favour joining NATO for strategic and geo-political reasons, fewer are happy about membership of the EU.

If social scars and disparities widen over the next four years for what many will perceive to be EU membership, Slovenians may become more reluctant to join an integrated Europe so soon after extricating themselves from the Yugoslav federation.
